Summary
19.1 What Is Working Capital?
Working capital is not only necessary to run a business; it is a resource that will expand and contract with
business cycles and must be carefully managed and monitored. The daily, weekly, and monthly needs of
business operations are met by cash. Financial managers understand the significance of net working capital
(current assets – current liabilities) and various liquidity ratios as they attempt to ensure that bills can be paid.
The cash conversion cycle and the cash budget provide additional working capital management tools.
19.2 What Is Trade Credit?
Trade credit is very prevalent in the business world, especially in B2B (business-to-business) transactions.
Many business exchanges (sales) could not take place without trade credit and the credit terms that are
offered. Like any component of working capital, trade credit must be planned and managed. The creditor (the
company granting the credit) does so based on an analysis of creditworthiness and must monitor payments
and manage slow-paying accounts. The debtor (accounts payable) needs to make payments on time to keep a
clean credit history and to take advantage of discounts.
19.3 Cash Management
Cash management is simply making sure you have enough cash to meet expected obligations and for
contingencies (unexpected or emergency cash needs). Excess cash should be invested low-risk and highly
liquid marketable securities. The cash budget is a critical tool of cash management.
19.4 Receivables Management
Accounts receivables are monitored by management with tools such as the ratios accounts receivable turnover
and average collection period and the aging of receivables. The credit managers’ mantra rings true: “The
older the receivable, the greater the likelihood that the account will not be collected.”
19.5 Inventory Management
Inventory, usually the least liquid of the current assets, presents its own set of management challenges.
Finding the optimal level of inventory is probably more of an art than a science. JIT helps to reduce the
investment in inventory and lower the costs of storage, but stockout costs can be very damaging to
profitability.
19.6 Using Excel to Create the Short-Term Plan
Short-term plans of a business are funded with cash, with cash budgets being a critical tool of planning. The
cash budget takes into account a target amount of cash, factoring in all the motives for holding cash. A cash
budget looks ahead—predicting cash inflows and outflows, allocating for minimum cash balances to be
maintained, and helping management determine short-term financing needed. Although it is the last budget
prepared, the preparation of the cash budget is an important financial planning exercise of companies small
and large.

Why It Matters
Each year, American Airlines consumes approximately four billion gallons of jet fuel.1 In the spring of 2018, jet
fuel prices rose from an average of $2.07 per gallon to a price of $2.19 per gallon.2 A $0.12-per-gallon increase
in the price of jet fuel may not seem significant, but on an annualized basis, a price increase of this magnitude
would increase the company’s jet fuel bill by approximately $500 million.
That added cost cuts into the profits of the company, leaving less money available to provide a return to the
company’s investors. Rising costs could even cause the business to become unprofitable and close, causing
many employees to lose their jobs. The financial managers of American Airlines are not able to control the
price of jet fuel. However, they must be aware of the risk that price volatility poses to the company and
consider prudent ways to manage this risk.

The Importance of Risk Management
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this section, you will be able to:
•
Describe risk in the context of financial management.
•

What Is Risk?
The job of the financial manager is to maximize the value of the firm for the owners, or shareholders, of the
company. The three major areas of focus for the financial manager are the size, the timing, and the riskiness
of the cash flows of the company. Broadly, the financial manager should work to
•
increase cash coming into the company and decrease cash going out of the company;
•
speed up cash coming into the company and slow down cash going out of the company; and
•
decrease the riskiness of both money coming in and money going out of the company.
The first item in this list is obvious. The more revenue a company has, the more profitable it will be.
Businesspeople talk about “top line” growth when discussing this objective because revenue appears at the
top of the company’s income statement. Also, the lower the company’s expenses, the more profitable the
company will be. When businesspeople talk about the “bottom line,” they are focused on what will happen to
a company’s net income. The net income appears at the bottom of the income statement and reflects the
amount of revenue left over after all of the company’s expenses have been paid.
The second item in the list—the speed at which money enters and exits the company—has been addressed
throughout this book. One of the basic principles of finance is the time value of money—the idea that a dollar

Businesspeople talk about “top line” growth when discussing this objective because revenue appears at the
top of the company’s income statement. Also, the lower the company’s expenses, the more profitable the
company will be. When businesspeople talk about the “bottom line,” they are focused on what will happen to
a company’s net income. The net income appears at the bottom of the income statement and reflects the
amount of revenue left over after all of the company’s expenses have been paid.
The second item in the list—the speed at which money enters and exits the company—has been addressed
throughout this book. One of the basic principles of finance is the time value of money—the idea that a dollar
received today is more valuable than a dollar received tomorrow. Many of the topics explored in this book
revolve around the issue of the time value of money.
The focus of this chapter is on the third item in the list: risk. In finance, risk is defined as uncertainty. Risk
occurs because you cannot predict the future. Compared to other business decisions, financial decisions are
generally associated with contracts in which the parties of the contract fulfill their obligations at different
points in time. If you choose to purchase a loaf of bread, you pay the baker for the bread as you receive the
bread; no future obligation arises for either you or the baker because of this purchase. If you choose to buy a
bond, you pay the issuer of the bond money today, and in return, the issuer promises to pay you money in the
future. The value of this bond depends on the likelihood that the promise will be fulfilled.
Because financial agreements often represent promises of future payment, they entail risk. Even if the party
that is promising to make a payment in the future is ethical and has every intention of honoring the promise,
things can happen that can make it impossible for them to do so. Thus, much of financial management hinges
on managing this risk.
Risk and Firm Value
You would expect the managers of Starbucks Corporation to know a lot about coffee. They must also know a
lot about risk. It is not surprising that the term coffee appears in the text of the company’s 2020 annual report
179 times, given that the company’s core business is coffee. It might be surprising, however, that the term risk
appears in the report 99 times.3 Given that the text of the annual report is less than 100 pages long, the word
risk appears, on average, more than once per page.
Starbucks faces a number of different types of risk. In 2020, corporations experienced an unprecedented risk
because of COVID-19. Coffee shops were forced to remain closed as communities experienced government-

immune to declining revenue due to the pandemic. As fewer people gathered in the workplace, Starbucks
experienced a declining number of to-go orders from meeting attendees. In addition, Starbucks locations

While COVID-19 brought discussions of risk to the forefront of everyday conversations, risk was an important
focus of companies such as Starbucks before the pandemic began. (The term risk appeared in the company’s

The investors in the company have allowed Starbucks to use its capital to lease storefronts, purchase espresso
machines, and obtain all of the assets necessary for the company to operate. Debt holders expect interest to
be paid and their principal to be returned. Stockholders expect a return on their investment. Because investors
are risk averse, the riskier they perceive the cash flows they will receive from the business to be, the higher the
expected return they will require to let the company use their money. This required return is a cost of doing
business. Thus, the riskier the cash flows of a company, the higher the cost of obtaining capital. As any cost of
operating a business increases, the value of the firm declines.

In the following sections, you will learn about some of the types of risk that firms commonly face. You will also
learn about ways in which firms can reduce their exposure to these risks. When firms take actions to reduce
their exposures to risk, they are said to be hedging. Firms hedge to try to protect themselves from losses.
Thus, in finance, hedging is a risk management tool.
Certain strategies are commonly used by firms to hedge risk, which is part of corporate financial management.
Many of these same strategies can be used by economic players who wish to speculate. Speculating occurs
when someone bets on a future outcome. It involves trying to predict the future and profit off of that
prediction, knowing that there is some risk that an incorrect prediction will lead to a loss. Speculators bet on
the future direction of an asset price. Thus, speculation involves directional bets.
If you are concerned that the price of hand sanitizer is going to rise because people are concerned about a
new virus and you purchase a few extra bottles to keep on your shelf “just in case,” you are hedging. If you see
this situation as a business opportunity and purchase bottles of hand sanitizer, hoping that you can sell them
on eBay in a few weeks at twice what you paid for them, you are speculating.
In the popular press, you will often hear of some of the strategies in this chapter discussed in terms of people
using them to speculate. In upper-level finance courses, these strategies are discussed in more depth,
including how they might be used to speculate. In this chapter, however, the focus is on the perspective of a
financial manager using these strategies to manage risk.

Long-Term Contracts
One method of hedging the risk of volatile input prices is for a firm to enter into long-term contracts with its
suppliers. Starbucks, for example, could enter into an agreement with a coffee farmer to purchase a particular
quantity of coffee beans at a predetermined price over the next several years.
These long-term contracts can benefit both the buyer and the seller. The buyer is concerned that rising
commodity prices will increase its cost of goods sold. The seller, however, is concerned that falling commodity
prices will mean lower revenue. By entering into a long-term contract, the buyer is able to lock in a price for its
raw materials and the seller is able to lock in its sales price. Thus, both parties are able to reduce uncertainty.

qa_pairs.question: What is commodity price risk and why is it significant for companies?
qa_pairs.answer: Commodity price risk refers to the volatility in the market price of raw materials that companies purchase to produce their products or provide their services. This risk is significant for companies because a change in the market price of these raw materials can significantly impact the profitability of a company. For example, Starbucks must purchase coffee beans to make its coffee drinks, and the price of coffee beans is highly volatile. The costs, and thus the profits, of Starbucks will vary greatly depending on if the company is paying less than $1.00 per pound for coffee or if it is paying three times that much.

qa_pairs.question: What are some strategies that firms can use to hedge commodity price risk?
qa_pairs.answer: Firms can use several strategies to hedge commodity price risk. One method is for a firm to enter into long-term contracts with its suppliers. By doing so, the firm can lock in a price for its raw materials, reducing uncertainty about the commodity price and thus reducing risk. Another strategy is vertical integration, where a firm takes control of the production process from start to finish, reducing its dependence on external suppliers and their prices. Futures contracts are also commonly used as a hedge. These are agreements to buy or sell a commodity at a predetermined price and date in the future, allowing a firm to protect itself from potential price increases or decreases.

These long-term contracts can benefit both the buyer and the seller. The buyer is concerned that rising

Vertical Integration
A common method of handling the risk associated with volatile input prices is vertical integration, which
involves the merger of a company and its supplier. For Starbucks, a vertical integration would involve
Starbucks owning a coffee bean farm. If the price of coffee beans rises, the firm’s costs increase and the
supplier’s revenues rise. The two companies can offset these risks by merging.
Although vertical integration can reduce commodity price risk, it is not a perfect hedge. Starbucks may
decrease its commodity price risk by purchasing a coffee farm, but that action may expose it to other risks,
such as land ownership and employment risk.
Futures Contracts
Another method of hedging commodity price risk is the use of a futures contract. A commodity futures
contract is designed to avoid some of the disadvantages of entering into a long-term contract with a supplier.
A futures contract is an agreement to trade an asset on some future date at a price locked in today. Futures
exist for a range of commodities, including natural resources such as oil, natural gas, coal, silver, and gold and
agricultural products such as soybeans, corn, wheat, rice, sugar, and cocoa.
Futures contracts are traded anonymously on an exchange; the market price is publicly observable, and the
market is highly liquid. The company can get out of the contract at any time by selling it to a third party at the
current market price.
A futures contract does not have the credit risk that a long-term contract has. Futures exchanges require
traders to post margin when buying or selling commodities futures contracts. The margin, or collateral, serves
as a guarantee that traders will honor their obligations. Additionally, through a procedure known as marking
to market, cash flows are exchanged daily rather than only at the end of the contract. Because gains and
losses are computed each day based on the change in the price of the futures contract, there is not the same
risk as with a long-term contract that the counterparty to the contract will not be able to fulfill their obligation.

qa_pairs.question: What is exchange rate risk and how does it impact businesses?
qa_pairs.answer: Exchange rate risk refers to the potential financial impact on a business due to fluctuations in the value of foreign currencies. This risk can affect businesses in several ways, such as transaction risk, translation risk, and economic risk. Transaction risk is the risk that the value of a business's expected receipts or expenses will change as a result of a change in currency exchange rates. For example, if a company like Starbucks agrees to pay a certain amount in a foreign currency for goods or services, the cost in their home currency can vary based on the exchange rate at the time of the transaction. Translation risk, on the other hand, is the risk that financial statements may be misstated due to changes in exchange rates. Economic risk is the risk that the overall economy of a foreign country will be negatively impacted, which can lead to a depreciation of the local currency and increased costs for the business.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between appreciation and depreciation of a currency?
qa_pairs.answer: Appreciation of a currency refers to a situation where one unit of a currency can buy more units of another currency. For example, if the US dollar appreciates relative to the Brazilian real, it means that more Brazilian reals can be purchased with one US dollar. Depreciation of a currency, on the other hand, refers to a situation where one unit of a currency can buy fewer units of another currency. For example, if the US dollar depreciates relative to the Brazilian real, it means that more US dollars are needed to purchase the same number of Brazilian reals.

qa_pairs.question: What is a natural hedge and how can it be used to manage exchange rate risk?
qa_pairs.answer: A natural hedge is a situation where a company's income and expenses are denominated in the same foreign currency. This can help to offset the impact of exchange rate fluctuations on the company's overall financial position. For example, if a company sells goods in a foreign country and also purchases raw materials from that same country, the income and expenses will be denominated in the same foreign currency. This can help to reduce the impact of exchange rate fluctuations on the company's profitability.

qa_pairs.question: What is a forward contract and how can it be used to manage exchange rate risk?
qa_pairs.answer: A forward contract is a financial instrument that allows parties to agree to exchange a specified amount of one currency for another at a future date at a predetermined exchange rate. This can be used to manage exchange rate risk by locking in the exchange rate for future transactions. For example, if a company knows that it will need to make a large payment in a foreign currency in the future, it can enter into a forward contract to purchase the necessary foreign currency at the current exchange rate, thereby protecting itself from potential fluctuations in the exchange rate.

qa_pairs.question: What are the characteristics of an option contract?
qa_pairs.answer: An option contract is a financial instrument that gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a specified amount of a particular asset at a predetermined price within a specified time period. The characteristics of an option contract include the strike price (the predetermined price at which the asset can be bought or sold), the expiration date (the date by which the option must be exercised), and the premium (the price paid for the option).

qa_pairs.question: What is the payoff to the holder of a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The payoff to the holder of a call option is the difference between the market price of the underlying asset and the strike price, if the market price is greater than the strike price. If the market price is less than the strike price, the payoff to the holder of a call option is zero.

qa_pairs.question: What is the payoff to the writer of a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The payoff to the writer of a call option is the difference between the strike price and the market price, if the market price is less than the strike price. If the market price is greater than the strike price, the writer of a call option must deliver the underlying asset to the holder and receive the difference between the market price and the strike price, minus the premium paid by the holder.

qa_pairs.question: What is the payoff to the holder of a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The payoff to the holder of a put option is the difference between the strike price and the market price, if the market price is less than the strike price. If the market price is greater than the strike price, the payoff to the holder of a put option is zero.

qa_pairs.question: What is the payoff to the writer of a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The payoff to the writer of a put option is the difference between the market price and the strike price, if the market price is greater than the strike price. If the market price is less than the strike price, the writer of a put option must buy the underlying asset from the holder and pay the difference between the market price and the strike price, minus the premium paid by the holder.

Economic Risk
Economic risk is the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact a business’s number of customers or its
sales. Even a company that is not involved in international transactions can face this type of risk. Consider a
company located in Mississippi that makes shirts using 100% US-grown cotton. All of the shirts are made in the
United States and sold to retail outlets in the United States. Thus, all of the company’s expenses and revenues
are in US dollars, and the company holds no assets outside of the United States.
Although this firm has no financial transactions involving international currency, it can be impacted by
changes in exchange rates. Suppose the US dollar strengthens relative to the Vietnamese dong. This will allow
US retail outlets to purchase more Vietnamese dong, and thus more shirts from Vietnamese suppliers, for the
same amount of US dollars. Because of this, the retail outlets experience a drop in the cost of procuring the
Vietnamese shirts relative to the shirts produced by the firm in Mississippi. The Mississippi company will lose
some of its customers to these Vietnamese producers simply because of a change in the exchange rate.
Hedging
Just as companies may practice hedging techniques to reduce their commodity risk exposure, they may
choose to hedge to reduce their currency risk exposure. The types of futures contracts that we discussed
earlier in this chapter exist for currencies as well as for commodities. A company that knows that it will need
Korean won later this year to purchase raw materials from a South Korean supplier, for example, can purchase
a futures contract for Korean won.
While futures contracts allow companies to lock in prices today for a future commitment, these contracts are
not flexible enough to meet the risk management needs of all companies. Futures contracts are standardized
contracts. This means that the contracts have set sizes and maturity dates. Futures contracts for Korean won,
for example, have a contract size of 125 million won. A company that needs 200 million won later this year
would need to either purchase one futures contract, hedging only a portion of its needs, or purchase two
futures contracts, hedging more than it needs. Either way, the company has remaining currency risk.
In this next section, we will explore some additional hedging techniques.

Suppose a company needs access to 200 million Korean won on March 1. In addition to a specified contract
size, currency futures contracts have specified days on which the contracts are settled. For most currency
futures contracts, this occurs on the third Wednesday of the month. If the company needed 125 million Korean
won (the basic contract size) on the third Wednesday of March (the standard settlement date), the futures

qa_pairs.question: What is the impact of exchange rate changes on the value of a company's assets as reported on the balance sheet?

When the exchange rate increases, the value of the company's assets increases as well, because more of the local currency is worth the same amount of the reporting currency. Conversely, when the exchange rate decreases, the value of the company's assets decreases, because more of the reporting currency is worth the same amount of the local currency. This decrease in the value of the company’s assets must be offset by a decrease in the stockholders’ equity for the balance sheet to balance. of the counterparty. If the company enters into a forward contract to purchase 200 million Korean won on

Natural Hedges
A hedge simply refers to a reduction in the risk or exposure that a company has to volatility and uncertainty.
We have been focusing on how a company might use financial market instruments to hedge, but sometimes a
company can use a natural hedge to mitigate risk. A natural hedge occurs when a business can offset its risk
simply through its own operations. With a natural hedge, when a risk occurs that would decrease the value of
a company, an offsetting event occurs within the firm that increases the value of the company.
As an example, consider a British-based travel agency. One of the major tours the company offers is a tour of
Italy. The company arranges for transportation, lodging, meals, and sightseeing for Brits to visit the highlights
of Rome, Florence, and Venice. Because the company charges customers in British pounds but must pay the
bus companies, hotels, and other service providers in Italy in euros, the travel agency faces significant
transaction exposure. If the value of the British pound depreciates after the company sets the price it will
charge for the tour but before it pays the Italian suppliers, the company will be harmed. In fact, if the British
pound depreciates by a great deal, the company could end up in a situation in which the British pounds it
collects are not enough to purchase the euros it needs to pay its suppliers.
The company could create a natural hedge by offering tours of London to individuals living in the European
Union. The travel agency could charge people who live in Germany, Italy, Spain, or any other country that has
the euro as its currency for a travel package to London. Then the agency would pay British restaurants, tour
guides, hotels, and bus companies in British pounds. This segment of the business also has currency risk. If
the British pound depreciates, the company gains because the euros it collects from its EU customers will
purchase more British pounds than before.

qa_pairs.question: What is a forward contract and how is it similar to a hotel room reservation?
qa_pairs.answer: A forward contract is a contract between two parties, such as a company and a bank, to exchange a specified amount of currency on a future date at a quoted rate. This contract is similar to agreeing with a hotel that you will arrive on a future (specified) date and pay the quoted price when you arrive. The hotel agrees to provide you the room on the specified date and cannot change the price of the room when you arrive. With a forward contract, both parties are under a contractual obligation to honor the contract, and the buyer cannot change their mind. This means that the seller, in this case the bank, will indeed make the exchange when the specified date arrives.

qa_pairs.question: What is counterparty risk in a forward contract?
qa_pairs.answer: Counterparty risk is a risk associated with a forward contract. It is the risk that the other party in the contract may not fulfill their obligations. For example, if a company enters into a forward contract to purchase a specified amount of currency from a bank on a future date, and the bank goes out of business before the specified date, the company will not be able to make the exchange with the nonexistent bank. This type of risk is not present in futures contracts, as the exchanges on which they are traded guard the purchaser of a futures contract from this type of risk by guaranteeing the contract.

qa_pairs.question: What is a natural hedge and how can a travel agency use it to mitigate risk?
qa_pairs.answer: A natural hedge is a risk reduction strategy that a company can use by offsetting its risk through its own operations. For example, a travel agency that offers tours in multiple countries can use a natural hedge to mitigate currency risk. If the travel agency charges customers in one currency but pays suppliers in another, it can create a situation where if the value of the currency it collects depreciates, an offsetting event occurs within the firm that increases the value of the currency it pays. As an example, a British-based travel agency offering tours of Italy could create a natural hedge by also offering tours of London to individuals living in the European Union. The travel agency would charge people who live in countries that use the euro for a travel package to London, and pay British restaurants, tour guides, hotels, and bus companies in British pounds. This way, if the British pound depreciates, the company gains because the euros it collects from its EU customers will purchase more British pounds than before, offsetting the loss from the tours of Italy.

qa_pairs.question: What is an option and what is the difference between exercising an option and owning an option?
qa_pairs.answer: An option is a financial instrument that gives the owner the right, but not the obligation, to purchase or sell an asset for a specified price at some future date. If the owner of an option decides to purchase or sell the asset according to the terms of the options contract, the owner is said to be exercising the option. Owning an option simply means that the owner has the right to exercise the option, but they are not obligated to do so.

Options
A financial option gives the owner the right, but not the obligation, to purchase or sell an asset for a specified
price at some future date. Options are considered derivative securities because the value of a derivative is
derived from, or comes from, the value of another asset.
Options Terminology
Specific terminology is used in the finance industry to describe the details of an options contract. If the owner
of an option decides to purchase or sell the asset according to the terms of the options contract, the owner is
said to be exercising the option. The price the option holder pays if purchasing the asset or receives if selling
the asset is known as the strike price or exercise price. The price the owner of the option paid for the option is
known as the premium.
An option contract will have an expiration date. The most common kinds of options are American options,
which allow the holder to exercise the option at any time up to and including the expiration date. Holders of
European options may exercise their options only on the expiration date. The labels American option and
European option can be confusing as they have nothing to do with the location where the options are traded.
Both American and European options are traded worldwide.
Option contracts are written for a variety of assets. The most common option contracts are options on shares
of stock. Options are traded for US Treasury securities, currencies, gold, and oil. There are also options on
agricultural products such as wheat, soybeans, cotton, and orange juice. Thus, options can be used by financial
managers to hedge many types of risk, including currency risk, interest rate risk, and the risk that arises from
fluctuations in the prices of raw materials.
Options are divided into two main categories, call options and put options. A call option gives the owner of
the option the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset. A put option gives the owner the
right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying asset.
Call Options
If a Korean company knows that it will need pay a $100,000 bill to a US supplier in six months, it knows how
many US dollars it will need to pay the bill. As a Korean company, however, its bank account is denominated in
Korean won. In six months, it will need to use its Korean won to purchase 100,000 US dollars.
The company can determine how many Korean won it would take to purchase $100,000 today. If the current
exchange rate is
, then it will need KWN 110,000,000 to pay the bill. The current
exchange rate is known as the spot rate.
The company, however, does not need the US dollars for another six months. The company can purchase a call
option, which is a contract that will allow it to purchase the needed US dollars in six months at a price stated in
the contract. This allows the company to guarantee a price for dollars in six months, but it does not obligate
the company to purchase the dollars at that price if it can find a better price when it needs the dollars in six
months.
The price that is in the contract is called the strike price (exercise price). Suppose the company purchases a
call contract for US dollars with a strike price of KWN 1,200/USD. While this contract would be for a set size, or
a certain number of US dollars, we will talk about this transaction as if it were per one US dollar to highlight
how options contracts work.

does not know what the spot exchange rate will be in three months, it faces transaction risk and may be

Interest Rate Risk
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this section, you will be able to:
•
Describe interest rate risk.
•
Explain how a change in interest rates changes the value of cash flows.
•
Describe the use of an interest rate swap.
An interest rate is simply the price of borrowing money. Just as other prices are volatile, interest rates are also
volatile. Just as volatility in other prices leads to uncertain cash flows for a company, volatility in interest rates
can also lead to uncertain cash flows.
Measuring Interest Rate Risk
Suppose that a company is supposed to pay a bill of $1,000 in 10 years. The present value of this bill depends
on the level of interest rates. If the interest rate is 5%, the present value of the bill is
. If
the interest rate rises to 6%, the present value of the bill is
. The increase in the interest
rate by 1% causes the present value of the expected cash flow to fall by

Interest rate risk can be highlighted by looking at bonds. Consider two $1,000 face value bonds with a 5%
coupon rate, paid semiannually. One of the bonds matures in five years, and the other bond matures in 30
years. If the market interest rate is 5%, each of these bonds will sell for face value, or $1,000. If, instead, the
market interest rate is 6%, the five-year bond will sell for $957.35 and the 30-year bond will sell for $861.62.
Notice that as the interest rate rises, the price of both of these bonds will fall. However, the price of the longer-
term bond will fall by more than the price of the shorter-term bond. The longer-term bond price will fall by
1.38%; the shorter-term bond price will fall by only 0.43%.
Consider two additional $1,000 face value bonds. The difference is that these bonds have a 6% coupon rate,
paid semiannually. If a bond has a 6% coupon rate and matures in five years, it will sell for $1,043.76 when the
market interest rate is 5%. A 30-year bond that matures in 30 years and has a 6% coupon rate will sell for
$1,154.54 when the market interest rate is 5%. However, if the interest rate in the economy is 6%, both of these
bonds will sell for a price of $1,000. The price of the five-year bond will drop by 4.19%; the price of the 30-year
bond will drop by 13.39%.

qa_pairs.question: What is the maximum profit a seller of a call option can make?
qa_pairs.answer: The maximum profit a seller of a call option can make is by the premium that was paid for the option; this occurs when the option is not exercised.

qa_pairs.question: What is the maximum loss a buyer of a call option can incur?
qa_pairs.answer: The maximum loss a buyer of a call option can incur is unlimited as the price of the underlying can rise indefinitely.

qa_pairs.question: What is the maximum profit a seller of a put option can make?
qa_pairs.answer: The maximum profit a seller of a put option can make is the premium received.

qa_pairs.question: What is the maximum loss a buyer of a put option can incur?
qa_pairs.answer: The maximum loss a buyer of a put option can incur is the difference between the strike price and the premium paid, as the price of the underlying can fall indefinitely.

qa_pairs.question: What is the right of the buyer of a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The right of the buyer of a call option is to buy the underlying asset at the strike price.

qa_pairs.question: What is the obligation of the seller of a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The obligation of the seller of a call option is to fulfill the contract should the buyer of the option choose to exercise the option.

qa_pairs.question: What is the right of the buyer of a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The right of the buyer of a put option is to sell the underlying asset to the seller at the strike price.

qa_pairs.question: What is the obligation of the seller of a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The obligation of the seller of a put option is to fulfill the contract should the buyer of the option choose to exercise the option.

qa_pairs.question: What is the benefit of buying a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The benefit of buying a call option is that the buyer can potentially profit from a rise in the price of the underlying asset without having to pay the full price for it.

qa_pairs.question: What is the harm of buying a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The harm of buying a call option is that the buyer can potentially lose the premium paid if the price of the underlying asset does not rise.

qa_pairs.question: What is the benefit of selling a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The benefit of selling a call option is that the seller can potentially earn the premium paid by the buyer.

qa_pairs.question: What is the harm of selling a call option?
qa_pairs.answer: The harm of selling a call option is that the seller can potentially lose the premium received if the buyer chooses to exercise the option and the price of the underlying asset rises.

qa_pairs.question: What is the benefit of buying a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The benefit of buying a put option is that the buyer can potentially profit from a fall in the price of the underlying asset without having to sell it at a loss.

qa_pairs.question: What is the harm of buying a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The harm of buying a put option is that the buyer can potentially lose the premium paid if the price of the underlying asset does not fall.

qa_pairs.question: What is the benefit of selling a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The benefit of selling a put option is that the seller can potentially earn the premium paid by the buyer.

qa_pairs.question: What is the harm of selling a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: The harm of selling a put option is that the seller can potentially lose the premium received if the buyer chooses to exercise the option and the price of the underlying asset falls.

Swap-Based Hedging
As the name suggests, a swap involves two parties agreeing to swap, or exchange, something. Generally, the
two parties, known as counterparties, are swapping obligations to make specified payment streams.
To illustrate the basics of how an interest rate swap works, let’s consider two hypothetical companies, Alpha
and Beta. Alpha is a strong, well-established company with a AAA (triple-A) bond rating. This means that Alpha
has the highest rating a company can have. With this high rating, Alpha can borrow at relatively low interest

that is widely quoted in the financial press. Historically, companies have often used the London Interbank
Offered Rate (LIBOR) as the benchmark rate. Because published quotes for LIBOR will be phased out by 2023,
firms are beginning to use alternative rates. As of yet, no single alternative has emerged as the most

Summary
20.1 The Importance of Risk Management
Risk arises due to uncertainty. The future is unpredictable. One job of the financial manager is to manage the
risks of both cash inflows and cash outflows. Investors are risk-averse. The riskier a firm’s cash flows are, the
higher the rate of return investors require to provide capital to the company.
20.2 Commodity Price Risk
Companies do not know how much they will have to pay for raw materials in future months. The price of raw
materials will change as economic conditions change, impacting a company’s cost of goods sold and profits.
Some ways that a company can hedge this risk are through vertical integration, long-term contracts, and
futures contracts.
20.3 Exchange Rates and Risk
Exchange rates are unpredictable. This leads to transaction risk, translation risk, and economic risk as currency
values change. A forward contract is an agreement between two parties to make an exchange at a particular
rate on a given date in the future. Companies can use options to mitigate the risks. A call option gives the
holder the right, but not the obligation, to purchase an underlying asset. A put option give the holder the right,
but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset.
20.4 Interest Rate Risk
When interest rates increase, the present value of future cash flows decreases. Duration is a measure of
interest rate risk. A swap involves two parties agreeing to exchange something, often specified payment
streams.

qa_pairs.question: What is an American option and what is its key characteristic?
qa_pairs.answer: An American option is a type of financial derivative that allows the holder to exercise the option at any time up to and including the exercise date. Its key characteristic is the flexibility it provides to the holder to exercise the option at their convenience.

qa_pairs.question: What does it mean for a currency to appreciate?
qa_pairs.answer: When a currency appreciates, it means that one unit of the currency will purchase more of a foreign currency than it did previously. This indicates a strengthening of the currency.

qa_pairs.question: What is a call option and what does it give the owner the right to do?
qa_pairs.answer: A call option is a financial derivative that gives the owner the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset at a specified price on some future date. It gives the owner the right to purchase the asset.

qa_pairs.question: What is a put option and what does it give the owner the right to do?
qa_pairs.answer: A put option is a financial derivative that gives the owner the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying asset at a specified price on some future date. It gives the owner the right to sell the asset.

qa_pairs.question: What is a derivative and how does it derive its value?
qa_pairs.answer: A derivative is a security that derives its value from another asset. Its value is determined by the value of the underlying asset.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between an American option and a European option?
qa_pairs.answer: The main difference between an American option and a European option is that an American option allows the holder to exercise the option at any time up to and including the exercise date, while a European option can only be exercised on the expiration date.

qa_pairs.question: What is the exercise price (strike price) in the context of an option?
qa_pairs.answer: The exercise price (strike price) is the price the option holder pays for the underlying asset when exercising an option.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a call option and a put option in terms of the right they give the holder?
qa_pairs.answer: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset, while a put option gives the holder the right to sell the underlying asset.

qa_pairs.question: What is a forward contract and what does it involve?
qa_pairs.answer: A forward contract is a contractual agreement between two parties to exchange a specified amount of assets on a specified future date. It involves agreeing to buy or sell a certain asset at a future date at a predetermined price.

qa_pairs.question: What is a futures contract and what does it involve?
qa_pairs.answer: A futures contract is a standardized contract to trade an asset on some future date at a price locked in today. It involves agreeing to buy or sell a certain asset at a future date at a predetermined price.

qa_pairs.question: What is hedging and what is its purpose?
qa_pairs.answer: Hedging is taking an action to reduce exposure to a risk. Its purpose is to protect against potential losses due to adverse price movements in the market.

qa_pairs.question: What is margin in the context of futures trading?
qa_pairs.answer: Margin is the collateral that must be posted to guarantee that a trader will honor a futures contract. It is a form of insurance for the counterparty in case the trader defaults on the contract.

qa_pairs.question: What is marking to market and what does it involve?
qa_pairs.answer: Marking to market is a procedure by which cash flows are exchanged daily for a futures contract, rather than at the end of the contract. It involves adjusting the value of the futures contract daily based on the current market price.

qa_pairs.question: What is a natural hedge and what does it involve?
qa_pairs.answer: A natural hedge is when a company offsets the risk that something will decrease in value by having a company activity that would increase in value at the same time. It involves using the natural operations of the business to offset potential risks.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between economic risk and transaction risk?
qa_pairs.answer: Economic risk is the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact the number of customers a business has or its sales. Transaction risk is the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact the value of a business’s expected receipts or expenses.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between translation risk and economic risk?
qa_pairs.answer: Translation risk is the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact the value of items on a company’s financial statements. Economic risk is the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact the number of customers a business has or its sales.

qa_pairs.question: What is vertical integration and what does it involve?
qa_pairs.answer: Vertical integration is the merger of a company with its supplier. It involves a company taking control of the supply chain by acquiring its suppliers.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between an American option and a European option?
qa_pairs.answer: An American option allows the holder to exercise the option at any time up to and including the expiration date, while a European option can only be exercised on the expiration date.

qa_pairs.question: Who has the right to buy and who has the right to sell an underlying asset in a call option and a put option?
qa_pairs.answer: In a call option, the holder has the right to buy the underlying asset, while in a put option, the holder has the right to sell the underlying asset.

qa_pairs.question: What are the three main categories of foreign exchange risk a company faces?
qa_pairs.answer: The three main categories of foreign exchange risk a company faces are economic risk, transaction risk, and translation risk.

qa_pairs.question: What does an exchange rate change from 1.20 to 1.15 mean?
qa_pairs.answer: An exchange rate change from 1.20 to 1.15 means that the currency being valued has depreciated relative to the US dollar.

qa_pairs.question: What will happen to the cost of US companies purchasing raw materials from South Korea if the exchange rate changes from 1.20 to 1.15?

qa_pairs.question: What is a foreign exchange forward contract?
qa_pairs.answer: A foreign exchange forward contract is a contractual agreement between two parties to exchange a specified amount of currencies on a future date.

qa_pairs.question: What is a measure of interest rate risk?
qa_pairs.answer: Duration is a measure of interest rate risk.

qa_pairs.question: What happens in a swap?
qa_pairs.answer: In a swap, two parties exchange specified payment streams.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between hedging and speculating with derivative securities?
qa_pairs.answer: Hedging with derivative securities is used to reduce the risk of adverse price movements, while speculating with derivative securities is used to profit from anticipated price movements.

qa_pairs.question: How can vertical integration be used as a method of hedging against commodity price risk?
qa_pairs.answer: Vertical integration can be used as a method of hedging against commodity price risk by controlling the supply chain from raw materials to finished goods, which allows a company to better predict and manage commodity prices.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a forward contract and a futures contract?
qa_pairs.answer: A forward contract is a customized contract between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a future date at a predetermined price, while a futures contract is a standardized contract traded on a futures exchange.

qa_pairs.question: Why are options considered to be a ‘zero-sum game’?
qa_pairs.answer: Options are considered to be a ‘zero-sum game’ because for every winner, there must be a loser. The total payoff to all option holders is equal to the total premiums collected, so the total payoff to the winners must equal the total premiums paid by the losers.

qa_pairs.question: If the Olive Orchard must pay 5.00 euros per liter of olive oil it purchases and it wants to purchase 7,000 liters of olive oil next year, how much will it cost the Olive Orchard (in euros) to purchase the 7,000 liters if the exchange rate remains constant at 0.900 euros per US dollar? If the exchange rate changes so that it costs 0.8599 euros to purchase 1 US dollar, how much will it cost to purchase the 7,000 liters of olive oil?
qa_pairs.answer: If the exchange rate remains constant at 0.900 euros per US dollar, the Olive Orchard will pay 5.00 euros per liter of olive oil times 7,000 liters, for a total cost of 35,000 euros. If the exchange rate changes so that it costs 0.8599 euros to purchase 1 US dollar, the Olive Orchard will pay 5.00 euros per liter of olive oil times 7,000 liters, but the total cost will be converted to US dollars using the new exchange rate of 0.8599 euros per US dollar. So, the total cost in US dollars will be 35,000 euros divided by 0.8599 US dollars per euro, for a total cost of approximately 40,666.67 US dollars.

qa_pairs.question: International Automobile Parts (IAP) holds a call option to purchase US dollars. The strike price on the call option is JPY 115/USD. IAP paid JPY 10 for the option. The spot price is JPY 120/USD, and the option expires today. Should IAP exercise the option? What is IAP’s payoff?
qa_pairs.answer: Since the spot price (JPY 120/USD) is greater than the strike price (JPY 115/USD), IAP should exercise the option. The payoff for IAP would be the difference between the spot price and the strike price, multiplied by the number of options held, minus the premium paid. So, if IAP holds one option, the payoff would be (JPY 120/USD - JPY 115/USD) times the number of options held, minus the premium paid, which is (JPY 120/USD - JPY 115/USD) times 1 minus JPY 10, for a payoff of approximately JPY 5.

qa_pairs.question: Global Producers (GP) holds a put option to sell US dollars. The strike price on the put option is JPY 114/USD. GP paid JPY 10 for the option. The spot price is JPY 120/USD, and the option expires today. Should GP exercise the option? What is GP’s payoff?

So, if GP holds one option, the payoff would be (JPY 114/USD - JPY 120/USD) times the number of options held, minus the premium paid, which is (JPY 120/USD - JPY 114/USD) times 1 minus JPY 10, for a payoff of approximately -JPY 6.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) and what is its role?
qa_pairs.answer: The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) is a non-governmental organization that regulates member brokerage firms and exchange markets in the United States. Its primary role is to protect investors by maintaining the fairness of the U.S. capital markets, ensuring that investors are provided with the information they need to make informed decisions, and helping to prevent fraudulent and unethical practices in the industry.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a financial analyst and a financial examiner?
qa_pairs.answer: A financial analyst is a professional who provides advice on investment decisions, evaluates securities, and conducts financial research. They analyze financial data to help individuals, corporations, and governments make informed investment decisions. On the other hand, a financial examiner is a professional who investigates the financial activities of businesses, financial institutions, and individuals to ensure compliance with laws and regulations. They are responsible for detecting fraud, assessing risk, and ensuring the financial stability of the entities they examine.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) and what is its role?
qa_pairs.answer: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) is a private, independent organization that establishes and improves accounting and financial reporting standards for the United States. Its primary role is to ensure that financial information is transparent, consistent, and useful to investors, creditors, and other users of financial reports. The FASB develops and issues accounting standards for a wide range of topics, including revenue recognition, leases, and financial instruments.

Its primary role is to protect investors by maintaining the fairness of the U.S. capital markets, ensuring that investors are provided with the information they need to make informed decisions, and helping to prevent fraudulent and unethical practices in the industry.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a financial instrument and a financial intermediary?
qa_pairs.answer: A financial instrument is a contract between parties that represents an ownership interest, a debt, or a derivative security. It can take various forms, such as stocks, bonds, options, and futures. A financial intermediary, on the other hand, is an entity that acts as a middleman in financial transactions, facilitating the flow of funds between borrowers and lenders, investors and issuers, and buyers and sellers. Examples of financial intermediaries include banks, insurance companies, and brokerage firms.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's long-term debt that pays a fixed interest rate and matures at a specific future date?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's long-term debt that pays a fixed interest rate and matures at a specific future date is a 'bond'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's equity that is not common stock and does not have voting rights?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's equity that is not common stock and does not have voting rights is 'preferred stock'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's assets that can be easily converted into cash within one year or less?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's assets that can be easily converted into cash within one year or less is 'current assets'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's liabilities that are due within one year or less?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's liabilities that are due within one year or less is 'current liabilities'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's long-term liabilities that are not due within one year?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's long-term liabilities that are not due within one year is 'noncurrent liabilities'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's assets that are not easily converted into cash within one year or less?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's assets that are not easily converted into cash within one year or less is 'noncurrent assets'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's expenses that are not in cash?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's expenses that are not in cash is 'noncash expenses'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's net operating profit after taxes?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's net operating profit after taxes is 'NOPAT'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's equity that is owned by the company's owners?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's equity that is owned by the company's owners is 'owner's equity'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's ratio of net income to total assets?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's ratio of net income to total assets is 'return on total assets'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's ratio of net income to equity?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's ratio of net income to equity is 'return on equity'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's ratio of sales to total assets?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's ratio of sales to total assets is 'asset turnover'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term used to describe a company's ratio of net income to total liabilities?
qa_pairs.answer: The term used to describe a company's ratio of net income to total liabilities is 'profit margin'.

qa_pairs.question: What is the term 'Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities' (TIPS) in the context of finance?
qa_pairs.answer: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, refer to a type of U.S. government bond that provides protection against inflation. These securities adjust their principal value and interest payments based on changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which is a measure of inflation. This means that as inflation increases, the principal and interest payments on TIPS also increase, providing a hedge against inflation for investors.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of the US Department of the Treasury?
qa_pairs.answer: The US Department of the Treasury is a federal executive department responsible for promoting economic prosperity and ensuring the financial security of the United States. Its main functions include formulating and implementing economic policy, collecting taxes, paying the nation's bills, and managing the public debt. It also oversees the production of currency and coinage, and enforces financial regulations.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between Treasury bills (T-bills) and Treasury bonds?
qa_pairs.answer: Treasury bills (T-bills) are short-term debt securities issued by the U.S. government with maturities of less than one year. They are sold at a discount to their face value and do not pay interest. Instead, the interest is implied in the discounted price. On the other hand, Treasury bonds are long-term debt securities with maturities of more than ten years. They are sold at face value and pay a fixed interest rate semi-annually. Unlike T-bills, Treasury bonds pay a regular income to the holder.

qa_pairs.question: What is the 'Treynor ratio' in finance?
qa_pairs.answer: The Treynor ratio is a measure of a portfolio's risk-adjusted return. It is calculated by subtracting the risk-free rate (usually the return on a U.S. Treasury bill) from the portfolio's return, and then dividing the result by the portfolio's beta (a measure of its systematic risk). The higher the Treynor ratio, the better the portfolio's performance relative to its risk.

qa_pairs.question: What is the 'yield curve' in finance?
qa_pairs.answer: The yield curve is a graphical representation of the interest rates for a given country's government bonds, plotted against their maturities. It shows the relationship between the yield (or return) and the term to maturity for bonds with different durations. A normal yield curve slopes upward, indicating that longer-term bonds have higher yields than shorter-term bonds, reflecting the higher risk associated with longer-term investments. An inverted yield curve, where shorter-term bonds have higher yields than longer-term bonds, is often seen as a predictor of an economic recession.
